scenario_stem:
Brackenfell Woodcraft is a family-run furniture business founded 9 years ago by Helen Marchetti in Country X. It employs 26 workers making handcrafted oak dining tables and chairs, with output of 140 tables a month and annual revenue of $620,000. It sells directly to local hotels, restaurants and homes across the capital region, and the workshop has three separate areas for cutting, sanding and assembly, with parts travelling 14 metres between them.

The production manager proposes kaizen, a programme of continuous small improvements costing about $6,500 a year in training and suggestion rewards. The alternative is a one-off investment of $95,000 in a computer-controlled sanding machine that would cut sanding time by 35%. Helen must decide which route to fund before the new financial year starts.

Reason 2: Kaizen costs very little in capital spending [k], at about $6,500 a year compared with a $95,000 machine [app].

Benefit 2: Kaizen builds a culture where all 26 workers contribute improvement ideas [k], applied across the 140 tables a month passing through cutting, sanding and assembly [app], cutting rework and defects over time [an].

It produces 9,500 meals a day for supermarkets and made revenue of $1.8 million last year. Fresh vegetables currently arrive in bulk every Monday, and demand peaks sharply before weekends. The operations manager proposes cell production, forming 6 cells of 6 workers, each completing a whole panel from start to finish. The finance director warns that reorganisation costs $38,000 and output would fall by 12% during changeover. Any defects reaching customers trigger penalty clauses. Quenby must vote on the proposal at its board meeting next month.

Customers currently wait 21 days for delivery, and two large cement works have threatened to switch suppliers. The mill runs two shifts, five days a week.

The general manager proposes lean production with demand-driven smaller runs, cutting warehouse space and order lead time. The sales manager warns that cement works buy in bulk and fears losing volume discounts worth $45,000 a year. scenario_stem:

The owner proposes lean production with a make-to-order approach for seasonal lines, making boxes only against confirmed retailer orders. The sales director warns this could leave shelves empty in peak weeks and lose impulse sales of about $48,000. The board must decide which system to use for the next Easter season, with production planning starting in December.

Daily output averages 3,200 litres, demand peaks in the hot summer months, and the business supplies hotel freezers and corner shops.

The production manager proposes kaizen workshops to redesign the ingredient route and add a mixing-schedule board, costing $3,400. The owner favours an $88,000 automated ingredient-dosing machine arriving in 8 months. Both options aim to cut waiting and defects. Silverbeck must choose one investment this quarter.

questions.question_text: Do you think Anvilbrook Bottling Co should accept the bespoke job production contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The contract pays $6.50 a bottle for 2,400 bottles, worth $15,600 [k], a high-margin one-off deal that could showcase the firm's cordials to a regional hotel group [app], potentially opening future contracts beyond the standard 15,000-bottle-a-week range [an]. However, hand-finishing removes up to two shifts from the lean line [k], risking waste above the usual 1.5% and delaying regular orders of 15,000 bottles a week [app], which could erode the reliability regular buyers rely on [an]. Overall, Anvilbrook should accept, but schedule the job after peak filling weeks [eval], securing $15,600 without sacrificing the lean flow that keeps waste at 1.5% [eval].
